screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will build a clear mental model of what Pacemaker does in a clustered environment and why it matters for high availability. Pacemaker is the intelligent orchestrator that watches nodes and services, makes decisions about where services should run, and moves them when failures occur. It relies on Corosync for cluster messaging and membership, but Pacemaker is responsible for declaring resources, their parameters, and rules that govern start order and co-location. You will see how the pcs utility records changes in the CIB, how to place the cluster into maintenance while you configure resources, and how to create two core primitives: a floating IP and a managed filesystem. I will show the typical commands you will use, explain monitoring intervals, and describe constraints such as prefers, order, and INFINITY colocation. You will also learn common pitfalls to avoid, like mounting a non-clustered filesystem on multiple nodes, and how to test failover safely. By the end you should be able to define primitive resources, add constraints to express dependencies, and verify behavior with pcs status. Consider what matters most in your environment: rapid detection, safe mounting of storage, and predictable failover.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Overview
Configuring Pacemaker for Resource Management
Define, constrain, and monitor resources so services fail over safely and predictably.
In this lesson

You will learn Pacemaker's role alongside Corosync, use pcs to write to the CIB, create IPaddr2 and Filesystem primitives, and apply location, order, and colocation constraints. Hands-on steps and verification are included.

Automated failover reduces downtime and aligns recovery with RTO goals.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Practice Checklist
Maintenance mode
Always set maintenance-mode=true before major changes and reset to false after testing. This prevents Pacemaker from acting on incomplete configs.

screens.title: Pacemaker and Corosync — Roles defined
screens.narratorSegment: Pacemaker and Corosync form a duo where each has a distinct responsibility. Corosync provides reliable messaging, node membership, and quorum information so every node agrees on who is in the cluster. Pacemaker consumes that membership view and becomes the decision engine: it monitors resources, decides where resources should run, and performs start/stop actions to keep services available. A clear example is failover: if Corosync reports a node is gone, Pacemaker consults the CIB and immediately attempts to start the affected resources on other eligible nodes. One common misconception is treating Pacemaker as a replacement for shared storage; it is not. Pacemaker orchestrates resource start and stop, but storage accessibility must be planned separately. Another frequent confusion is assuming CIB writes are local; the CIB is replicated across nodes, so using pcs modifies a cluster-wide configuration. The practical significance is operational: you must ensure both reliable messaging and well-defined resources. If either side is misconfigured—network partitions in Corosync or incorrect resource parameters in Pacemaker—failover will not behave predictably. Reflect on this: how does your environment ensure both reliable membership and correct resource actions?

keyIdea.text: Corosync supplies membership and messaging; Pacemaker uses that data to orchestrate resource start/stop and failover according to the CIB.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Pacemaker & Corosync
Claim

Corosync handles cluster messaging and membership; Pacemaker makes orchestration decisions and acts on resources in response to that state.

Example scenario
If a node loses network connectivity, Corosync detects the membership change and Pacemaker relocates resources to healthy nodes.
Misconception
Pacemaker is not a storage system. Ensure storage is cluster-aware or only mounted on one node at a time to prevent corruption.
Key Takeaway
Both messaging and orchestration must be correct for safe failover; problems in either cause unpredictable behavior.
Annotated roles
Corosync
Reliable messaging, membership, quorum.
Pacemaker
Resource orchestration, monitoring, and recovery decisions based on the CIB.
CIB
Replicated XML configuration that records resources and constraints for every node to act upon.

screens.title: Using pcs and the CIB
screens.narratorSegment: The pcs utility is your primary interface to Pacemaker configuration and it writes changes into the Cluster Information Base, the replicated XML store every node consults. When you issue a pcs resource create or pcs constraint command, pcs updates the CIB and Pacemaker on each node acts on that new configuration. A recommended process when making multiple interdependent changes is: first enter maintenance mode so Pacemaker will not attempt to start incomplete resource groups; second, create or modify resources and constraints; third, verify the CIB and resource status; and finally exit maintenance mode to allow Pacemaker to manage resources normally. For example, set maintenance-mode=true before creating both a filesystem resource and an IP resource that depend on each other. After you confirm both resources and their constraints appear in the CIB and are syntactically correct, set maintenance-mode=false. One misconception is skipping maintenance mode during risky changes and assuming Pacemaker will not act – Pacemaker may attempt to start partially configured resources and generate recovery events. The safe sequence protects production services while you configure and validate each step. Using pcs and the CIB means enter maintenance mode, perform configuration changes with pcs (updates cib), verify status, then exit maintenance mode to resume orchestration.. In practical terms, how pcs updates the replicated cluster information base and why maintenance mode matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Enter maintenance mode, perform configuration changes with pcs (updates CIB), verify status, then exit maintenance mode to resume orchestration.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Using pcs & the CIB
Recommended sequence
1. Enter maintenance
sudo pcs property set maintenance-mode=true — prevents Pacemaker from acting on incomplete configs while you make multiple changes.
2. Create resources
Use pcs resource create to add primitives; pcs writes changes to the CIB and Pacemaker on each node will later act on them.
3. Verify
Run pcs status and inspect the CIB to ensure resources and constraints are correct before enabling orchestration.
4. Exit maintenance
sudo pcs property set maintenance-mode=false — allow Pacemaker to start and monitor resources using the updated CIB.
Why it matters
Maintenance mode prevents premature recovery attempts while interdependent resources are being created. This reduces the risk of partial starts or repeated restart loops that complicate debugging.
Quick commands
sudo pcs property set maintenance-mode=true
# make changes
sudo pcs property set maintenance-mode=false
sudo pcs status
sudo pcs status resources
sudo pcs constraint
Common mistake
Skipping maintenance mode during multi-step configuration can lead to Pacemaker acting on incomplete resource sets and generating confusing failures.

screens.title: Resource Agents and Primitive Resources
screens.narratorSegment: A resource agent is a script that knows how to start, stop, and monitor a specific type of service or object. They live in standard paths such as the Open Cluster Framework directory and each agent implements the actions Pacemaker needs to control the resource. In Pacemaker terminology a primitive resource is a single, standalone managed unit created with pcs resource create. Examples you will use include IPaddr2 for a floating IP, Filesystem for mounting a device at a mount point, apache for a web server, and MariaDB for a database process. When defining a primitive you provide the resource agent type, a unique name, and any required parameters such as ip and cidr_netmask for IPaddr2, or device, directory, and fstype for Filesystem. A typical misconception is assuming an agent will magically handle all filesystem quirks; the agent needs a correct device path and an accessible filesystem. If the device is missing or inaccessible on a node, Pacemaker cannot mount it and related resources may fail. Keep this in mind when writing resource definitions and testing them in your lab.

keyIdea.text: Resource agents encapsulate start/stop/monitor logic; primitive resources are single managed units created with pcs and parameterized for each environment.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Resource Agents
What they do

Resource agents implement the operations Pacemaker uses to control resources: start, stop, and monitor. They are typically provided under the OCF namespace and referenced when creating primitives.

Common primitive types
  • IPaddr2 — floating IP addresses
  • Filesystem — mount a block device to a directory
  • apache, MariaDB — service-specific agents
Example
A filesystem resource must reference a device path available to all nodes and a mount directory that Pacemaker will manage on whichever node owns the resource.
Example resource definition
sudo pcs resource create SharedFS ocf:heartbeat:Filesystem device="/dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_data" directory="/mnt/data" fstype="xfs" op monitor interval=20s
Pitfall
Do not mount a non-clustered filesystem simultaneously on multiple nodes. That leads to corruption. Use a clustered filesystem or ensure only one node mounts it at a time.

screens.title: Create a Floating IP with pcs
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through creating a floating IP resource using pcs and the IPaddr2 resource agent. The example command demonstrates the required pieces: a unique resource name, the OCF agent type, parameters for the IP and netmask, and an operation that defines monitoring frequency. When you run the command Pacemaker records the resource in the CIB and will try to start it on an eligible node. Here is a concrete command you will use in the lab. As you read the command, note that IPaddr2 needs the ip and cidr_netmask parameters; without correct network parameters the resource cannot be assigned to an interface. Also the op monitor interval controls how often Pacemaker verifies the floating IP is present. A common misconception is that the monitoring interval only matters for detection; it also affects scheduler activity and agent invocation frequency. After creating the resource, verify it with pcs status resources and confirm the node owning the resource. Consider: if the IP disappears from the active interface, Pacemaker will try to bring it back or move it to a healthy node. Create a Floating IP with pcs means pcs resource create <name> ocf:heartbeat:ipaddr2 ip=<ip> cidr_netmask=<mask> op monitor interval=<seconds> — this writes a floating ip primitive to the cib.. In practical terms, command breakdown and parameters for ipaddr2. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Create Floating IP
Example command
sudo pcs resource create VirtualIP ocf:heartbeat:IPaddr2 ip=192.168.1.100 cidr_netmask=24 op monitor interval=10s
Parts explained
  • VirtualIP: unique resource name
  • ocf:heartbeat:IPaddr2: agent type and provider
  • ip / cidr_netmask: address and subnet
  • op monitor interval: monitoring frequency
Practical note
Ensure the IP is routable in your cluster network and not already used. If the IP cannot be assigned to the node interface, the agent will fail to start the resource.
Verification
sudo pcs status resources
# shows which node currently owns VirtualIP
Key Takeaway
IPaddr2 provides a floating IP that Pacemaker will move between nodes according to constraints and node health; monitoring interval affects detection speed and load.

screens.title: Create a Shared Filesystem Resource
screens.narratorSegment: Managing shared storage is a common requirement for HA services. Pacemaker can manage a Filesystem primitive that mounts a block device on the active node. When creating such a resource you must supply the device path, the directory to mount, the file system type, and a monitoring interval. For example, a safe demonstration uses a dedicated block device formatted with XFS and a mount point created on all nodes. The critical operational constraint is that the underlying storage must be accessible from all nodes but mounted by Pacemaker on only one node at a time unless you are using a clustered filesystem like GFS2. A frequent and dangerous mistake is attempting to mount the same non-clustered filesystem concurrently on multiple nodes; that risks data corruption. After creating the Filesystem resource, use pcs status resources to confirm ownership. If mounting fails, review device paths and permissions; missing device nodes or incorrect fstype are common causes. Always validate the device exists and is formatted on each node before letting Pacemaker mount it. Create a Shared Filesystem Resource means ensure the block device exists on all nodes and only allow pacemaker to mount it on one node at a time unless using a clustered filesystem.. In practical terms, filesystem resource definition and safe storage considerations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Shared Filesystem
Command example
sudo pcs resource create SharedFS ocf:heartbeat:Filesystem device="/dev/mapper/vg_data-lv_data" directory="/mnt/data" fstype="xfs" op monitor interval=20s
Important check
Confirm the device path exists and is formatted on every node before creating the resource. Also ensure /mnt/data exists on every node.
Storage considerations
  • Shared storage must be accessible from all nodes.
  • Non-clustered filesystems should be mounted by Pacemaker on only one node at a time.
  • Use clustered filesystems like GFS2 when concurrent mounts are required.
Common mistake
Mounting a non-clustered filesystem on multiple nodes simultaneously can corrupt data. Pacemaker prevents this when properly configured with a filesystem primitive.

screens.title: Monitoring frequency — balancing detection and load
screens.narratorSegment: Every primitive can include an op monitor interval that tells Pacemaker how often to run the resource agent's monitor action. This parameter balances two competing needs: quick detection of failure and avoiding excessive agent invocations that add C P U or input and output overhead. If you set a very short interval, the agent will run frequently, which may place unnecessary load on the cluster and on the resource itself. If you set a very long interval, detection and recovery will be slower, increasing the Recovery Time Objective. Consider the VirtualIP example with a 10-second monitor: this is responsive and reasonable for a simple IP check. For heavier-weight checks, like verifying a database process with complex probes, a longer interval may be appropriate. A misconception is assuming shorter is always better; in practice you must measure the agent's cost and the acceptable detection latency for your application. Start with sensible defaults like 10–20 seconds for simple resources, then tune based on observed behavior in your environment and lab testing. Monitoring frequency — balancing detection and load means op monitor interval determines detection latency versus system overhead; choose an interval that balances rto needs and agent cost.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Monitoring Interval
Short interval (responsive)
Pros: fast detection and quicker failover. Cons: higher CPU and I/O from frequent agent runs; may impact resource performance.
Example
VirtualIP with op monitor interval=10s detects address loss quickly and initiates failover.
Long interval (economical)
Pros: less overhead from monitoring. Cons: longer detection time increases service downtime before recovery.
Guideline
Pick intervals based on agent cost and acceptable downtime. Simple resources: shorter intervals. Costly probes: longer intervals.
Key Takeaway
Balance detection speed and resource overhead with a tuned op monitor interval; test in a lab to find safe defaults for your services.

screens.title: Location Constraints and Preferences
screens.narratorSegment: Location constraints let you influence or enforce where resources run. A preference like prefers with a positive score nudges the scheduler to place the resource on a chosen node but does not absolutely prevent placement elsewhere. For example, sudo pcs constraint location VirtualIP prefers node1. example. com=50 makes node1 more desirable for VirtualIP. Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Location Constraints
Soft preference example
# Prefer VirtualIP to run on node1
sudo pcs constraint location VirtualIP prefers node1.example.com=50
The score 50 increases node1's attractiveness. If node1 fails, the resource will run elsewhere.
Hard pin and avoidance
Hard pin
Use a strong score or INFINITY in other constraints to require a resource to run on a specific node.
Tip
Avoid conflicting location constraints. If two constraints point to different preferred nodes with similar scores, evaluate how the scheduler resolves them.

screens.title: Order and Colocation Constraints
screens.narratorSegment: Order and colocation constraints express dependencies between resources. An order constraint enforces that one resource starts before another; for instance SharedFS then VirtualIP ensures the filesystem is mounted before the IP is brought online. Colocation ties resources to the same host so that related services and their IPs move together. For a strict requirement use INFINITY, as in sudo pcs constraint colocation add VirtualIP with SharedFS INFINITY. This guarantees both resources run on the same node. If you only want a strong preference, use a positive score like 100 instead of INFINITY. A misconception here is expecting order constraints to automatically force co-location; order only establishes sequence, not placement. You often need both order and colocation to ensure a filesystem mounts on the same node before services that need it start. When designing constraints consider failure modes: if SharedFS fails to mount, order constraints will cause VirtualIP to remain stopped until the dependency is resolved. Test this behavior in a lab to ensure the combined constraints produce the intended startup and failover sequences. Order and Colocation Constraints means use order constraints for sequence and colocation for placement. combine both when a resource must be mounted before another starts on the same node.. In practical terms, ensuring resources start in sequence and run together safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Order example
sudo pcs constraint order SharedFS then VirtualIP
This ensures the filesystem is started before the IP is created, avoiding a service that comes up before its storage is available.
Colocation example

INFINITY forces both resources to run on the same node. Use positive scores for preferences instead of hard requirements when needed.

screens.title: Hands-on: Creating and Constraining a Basic HA Service
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on flow collects the commands and checks you will perform in the lab. Start by entering maintenance mode so Pacemaker will not act on partial changes. Create the VirtualIP resource and the SharedFS filesystem resource with correct parameters—device path, directory, and fstype. Then add a colocation constraint so the two resources run together and an order constraint so the filesystem starts before the IP. Exit maintenance mode to allow Pacemaker to start and monitor the resources. Verify state with pcs status and pcs status resources, and then test failover either by moving the resource manually or by stopping Pacemaker on the original node. When you move resources, ensure both resources move together as required by the colocation constraint. A common mistake in labs is forgetting to create the mount point or format the device on both nodes; if that happens Pacemaker will fail to mount and related resources will remain inactive. Use these steps to validate the complete lifecycle: create, constrain, verify, test, and observe both status and logs for troubleshooting. content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.3 › Hands-on Activity
Step-by-step commands
sudo pcs property set maintenance-mode=true
sudo pcs resource create VirtualIP ocf:heartbeat:IPaddr2 ip=192.168.1.100 cidr_netmask=24 op monitor interval=10s
sudo pcs resource create SharedFS ocf:heartbeat:Filesystem device="/dev/sdb1" directory="/mnt/data" fstype="xfs" op monitor interval=20s
sudo pcs constraint colocation add VirtualIP with SharedFS INFINITY
sudo pcs constraint order SharedFS then VirtualIP
sudo pcs property set maintenance-mode=false
sudo pcs status
sudo pcs status resources
sudo pcs constraint
Testing failover
Move resources manually or stop Pacemaker on the active node to simulate failure. For example: sudo pcs resource move VirtualIP node2.example.com. Observe that SharedFS and VirtualIP move together when colocation and order are correct.
Checklist
  • Device formatted and mount point created on all nodes
  • Constraints present and verified
  • Maintenance mode used for safe configuration

screens.title: Monitoring, Logs, and Common Troubles
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting Pacemaker configurations often involves three inspection points: the CIB, Pacemaker and Corosync logs, and the current cluster status as reported by pcs. If a resource won't start, first confirm the resource agent parameters and that the underlying device or service is present. Use sudo pcs status and sudo pcs status resources to see which node owns a resource and recent errors. Next, check journalctl for pacemaker and corosync services to find agent failures or membership errors. Common problems include incorrect device paths for Filesystem resources, missing mount points, incorrect fstype, or conflicting constraints that leave no eligible node. Another frequent issue is forgetting that prefers is not a hard pin; constraints with low scores may be overridden by node failures or other scoring. When diagnosing, reproduce the failure in a non-production lab and review the CIB for syntax or parameter mistakes. If monitoring indicates repeated restarts, consider raising the monitor interval or examining the agent's exit codes. End your investigation by testing a manual move and watching that constraints are honored; that often reveals dependency or parameter issues you can fix.

  • Run sudo pcs status and sudo pcs status resources to observe ownership and failures.

Use status, CIB verification, and logs together to identify misconfigured parameters or constraint conflicts, and always test fixes in a non-production environment first.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will build a clear mental model of what Pacemaker does in a clustered environment and why it matters for high availability. Pacemaker is the intelligent orchestrator that watches nodes and services, makes decisions about where services should run, and moves them when failures occur. It relies on Corosync for cluster messaging and membership, but Pacemaker is responsible for declaring resources, their parameters, and rules that govern start order and co-location. You will see how the pcs utility records changes in the CIB, how to place the cluster into maintenance while you configure resources, and how to create two core primitives: a floating IP and a managed filesystem. I will show the typical commands you will use, explain monitoring intervals, and describe constraints such as prefers, order, and INFINITY colocation. You will also learn common pitfalls to avoid, like mounting a non-clustered filesystem on multiple nodes, and how to test failover safely. By the end you should be able to define primitive resources, add constraints to express dependencies, and verify behavior with pcs status. Consider what matters most in your environment: rapid detection, safe mounting of storage, and predictable failover.

By the end of these exercises you should be able to explain Pacemaker's role, use pcs to define primitive resources, apply constraints to control placement and ordering, and monitor and troubleshoot resource behavior. First, you will learn how Pacemaker works with Corosync to provide membership and messaging while Pacemaker acts on that information to start, stop, and move resources. Second, you will gain hands-on competence with pcs and the Cluster Information Base so you can make reproducible configuration changes. Third, you will learn practical constraint types—location, order, and colocation—that express preferences and hard requirements for where services run. Finally, you will practice verifying resource state and looking at logs and status output to diagnose misconfigurations. Each objective is chosen because these are the operations administrators perform daily when keeping services highly available. For example, creating an IPaddr2 resource and adding an order constraint prevents services from starting before their filesystem is mounted. Keep in mind a common misconception: a preference is not a guarantee. Prefers influence placement but do not force it; use INFINITY or negative scores for hard rules.

This second objectives slide gives practical assessment anchors you can use when practising. For each objective imagine a quick test: show the CIB after creating a resource to verify pcs recorded the change; place the cluster into maintenance mode before you make multiple related changes and then exit maintenance when done; create an IPaddr2 resource and confirm pcs status resources shows which node owns it; and add colocation and order constraints, then manually move a resource to verify both resources move together. Each of these is a lightweight validation you can run in a lab. A common misconception is assuming a preference equals a hard rule: prefers influence placement but do not prevent the scheduler from choosing another node when scores and failures interact. For a must-have relationship use INFINITY for colocation or negative INFINITY to forbid co-location. These checks will help you avoid mistakes that cause downtime or data corruption.

Pacemaker and Corosync form a duo where each has a distinct responsibility. Corosync provides reliable messaging, node membership, and quorum information so every node agrees on who is in the cluster. Pacemaker consumes that membership view and becomes the decision engine: it monitors resources, decides where resources should run, and performs start/stop actions to keep services available. A clear example is failover: if Corosync reports a node is gone, Pacemaker consults the CIB and immediately attempts to start the affected resources on other eligible nodes. One common misconception is treating Pacemaker as a replacement for shared storage; it is not. Pacemaker orchestrates resource start and stop, but storage accessibility must be planned separately. Another frequent confusion is assuming CIB writes are local; the CIB is replicated across nodes, so using pcs modifies a cluster-wide configuration. The practical significance is operational: you must ensure both reliable messaging and well-defined resources. If either side is misconfigured—network partitions in Corosync or incorrect resource parameters in Pacemaker—failover will not behave predictably. Reflect on this: how does your environment ensure both reliable membership and correct resource actions?

The pcs utility is your primary interface to Pacemaker configuration and it writes changes into the Cluster Information Base, the replicated XML store every node consults. When you issue a pcs resource create or pcs constraint command, pcs updates the CIB and Pacemaker on each node acts on that new configuration. A recommended process when making multiple interdependent changes is: first enter maintenance mode so Pacemaker will not attempt to start incomplete resource groups; second, create or modify resources and constraints; third, verify the CIB and resource status; and finally exit maintenance mode to allow Pacemaker to manage resources normally. For example, set maintenance-mode=true before creating both a filesystem resource and an IP resource that depend on each other. After you confirm both resources and their constraints appear in the CIB and are syntactically correct, set maintenance-mode=false. One misconception is skipping maintenance mode during risky changes and assuming Pacemaker will not act – Pacemaker may attempt to start partially configured resources and generate recovery events. The safe sequence protects production services while you configure and validate each step. Using pcs and the CIB means enter maintenance mode, perform configuration changes with pcs (updates cib), verify status, then exit maintenance mode to resume orchestration.. In practical terms, how pcs updates the replicated cluster information base and why maintenance mode matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A resource agent is a script that knows how to start, stop, and monitor a specific type of service or object. They live in standard paths such as the Open Cluster Framework directory and each agent implements the actions Pacemaker needs to control the resource. In Pacemaker terminology a primitive resource is a single, standalone managed unit created with pcs resource create. Examples you will use include IPaddr2 for a floating IP, Filesystem for mounting a device at a mount point, apache for a web server, and MariaDB for a database process. When defining a primitive you provide the resource agent type, a unique name, and any required parameters such as ip and cidr_netmask for IPaddr2, or device, directory, and fstype for Filesystem. A typical misconception is assuming an agent will magically handle all filesystem quirks; the agent needs a correct device path and an accessible filesystem. If the device is missing or inaccessible on a node, Pacemaker cannot mount it and related resources may fail. Keep this in mind when writing resource definitions and testing them in your lab.

Let's walk through creating a floating IP resource using pcs and the IPaddr2 resource agent. The example command demonstrates the required pieces: a unique resource name, the OCF agent type, parameters for the IP and netmask, and an operation that defines monitoring frequency. When you run the command Pacemaker records the resource in the CIB and will try to start it on an eligible node. Here is a concrete command you will use in the lab. As you read the command, note that IPaddr2 needs the ip and cidr_netmask parameters; without correct network parameters the resource cannot be assigned to an interface. Also the op monitor interval controls how often Pacemaker verifies the floating IP is present. A common misconception is that the monitoring interval only matters for detection; it also affects scheduler activity and agent invocation frequency. After creating the resource, verify it with pcs status resources and confirm the node owning the resource. Consider: if the IP disappears from the active interface, Pacemaker will try to bring it back or move it to a healthy node. Create a Floating IP with pcs means pcs resource create <name> ocf:heartbeat:ipaddr2 ip=<ip> cidr_netmask=<mask> op monitor interval=<seconds> — this writes a floating ip primitive to the cib.. In practical terms, command breakdown and parameters for ipaddr2. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Managing shared storage is a common requirement for HA services. Pacemaker can manage a Filesystem primitive that mounts a block device on the active node. When creating such a resource you must supply the device path, the directory to mount, the file system type, and a monitoring interval. For example, a safe demonstration uses a dedicated block device formatted with XFS and a mount point created on all nodes. The critical operational constraint is that the underlying storage must be accessible from all nodes but mounted by Pacemaker on only one node at a time unless you are using a clustered filesystem like GFS2. A frequent and dangerous mistake is attempting to mount the same non-clustered filesystem concurrently on multiple nodes; that risks data corruption. After creating the Filesystem resource, use pcs status resources to confirm ownership. If mounting fails, review device paths and permissions; missing device nodes or incorrect fstype are common causes. Always validate the device exists and is formatted on each node before letting Pacemaker mount it. Create a Shared Filesystem Resource means ensure the block device exists on all nodes and only allow pacemaker to mount it on one node at a time unless using a clustered filesystem.. Every primitive can include an op monitor interval that tells Pacemaker how often to run the resource agent's monitor action. This parameter balances two competing needs: quick detection of failure and avoiding excessive agent invocations that add C P U or input and output overhead. If you set a very short interval, the agent will run frequently, which may place unnecessary load on the cluster and on the resource itself. If you set a very long interval, detection and recovery will be slower, increasing the Recovery Time Objective. Consider the VirtualIP example with a 10-second monitor: this is responsive and reasonable for a simple IP check. For heavier-weight checks, like verifying a database process with complex probes, a longer interval may be appropriate. A misconception is assuming shorter is always better; in practice you must measure the agent's cost and the acceptable detection latency for your application. Start with sensible defaults like 10–20 seconds for simple resources, then tune based on observed behavior in your environment and lab testing. Troubleshooting Pacemaker configurations often involves three inspection points: the CIB, Pacemaker and Corosync logs, and the current cluster status as reported by pcs. If a resource won't start, first confirm the resource agent parameters and that the underlying device or service is present. Use sudo pcs status and sudo pcs status resources to see which node owns a resource and recent errors. Next, check journalctl for pacemaker and corosync services to find agent failures or membership errors. Common problems include incorrect device paths for Filesystem resources, missing mount points, incorrect fstype, or conflicting constraints that leave no eligible node. Another frequent issue is forgetting that prefers is not a hard pin; constraints with low scores may be overridden by node failures or other scoring. When diagnosing, reproduce the failure in a non-production lab and review the CIB for syntax or parameter mistakes. If monitoring indicates repeated restarts, consider raising the monitor interval or examining the agent's exit codes. End your investigation by testing a manual move and watching that constraints are honored; that often reveals dependency or parameter issues you can fix.

Keep these short definitions in mind as you design HA services. The CIB is the replicated XML database where Pacemaker stores its configuration so every node acts from the same plan. A resource is any managed object—an IP, filesystem, or service—that Pacemaker controls. A resource agent is the script Pacemaker uses to start, stop, and monitor a specific resource type. Understanding these three concepts is foundational: the CIB holds the plan, resource agents implement actions, and resources are the units being controlled. When you write configuration with pcs you are updating the CIB and instructing Pacemaker how to act.
